quote: Anger exists in Homo sapiens because angry ancestors had more kids. There’s no other way it could have gotten there.
content: There are several other ways, and every one of them is textbook evolutionary biology. A trait can be present because it is a by-product of something else that was selected, because of pleiotropy, because of drift, or because it is an inherited feature of a lineage that was never selected against; the leading evolutionary psychologists themselves published a paper distinguishing adaptations from exaptations and spandrels and cautioning against assuming the first (Buss et al. 1998). Anger-like approach-and-threat responses are shared across mammals, so "angry ancestors had more kids" may be true of some pre-primate lineage in a way that says little about the human emotion. The essay's "no other way" is the adaptationist fallacy that Gould & Lewontin (1979) named, stated in its purest form.

quote: Some brain organs are directly reproductive, like lust; others are indirectly reproductive, like anger.
content: There is no anger organ. Meta-analysis of neuroimaging finds no brain region or network that is consistently and specifically activated by any single discrete emotion; the same regions participate in many emotions and in non-emotional processing (Lindquist et al. 2012). The picture of the brain as a collection of dedicated evolved modules is the massive-modularity thesis, and it is contested on both neural and computational grounds: cortical regions are reused across wildly different tasks (Anderson 2010), and the defenders of modularity have had to redefine "module" so loosely that the thesis loses much of its content (Barrett & Kurzban 2006). The organ metaphor smuggles in a contested architecture as if it were anatomy.

quote: The woman is attracted to his confident smile and firm manner, cues to high status, which in the ancestral environment would have signified the ability to provide resources for children.
content: The sex-differentiated mate-preference story comes from self-report surveys (Buss 1989), and it has two well-documented problems. First, stated preferences do not predict whom people are actually attracted to: in speed-dating studies, the sex difference in weighting status versus attractiveness disappears when real partners rather than hypothetical ones are being evaluated (Eastwick & Finkel 2008). Second, the size of the sex difference across nations tracks the nations' gender inequality, shrinking sharply where women have economic independence, which is what a social-role account predicts and an ancestral-adaptation account does not (Zentner & Mitura 2012). The vignette narrates a contested hypothesis as if it were the woman's neural wiring.

quote: Like “IRC chat” or “TCP/IP protocol,” the phrase “reproductive organ” is redundant. All organs are reproductive organs.
content: Cute, but it defines away a real distinction and ignores everything that is not an adaptation. The appendix, the plantar muscles, the genes for a functional vitamin-C pathway that primates broke and never repaired, and much of the genome are present not because they contributed to ancestral reproduction but because nothing removed them; non-adaptive evolution is the null hypothesis that adaptive stories must beat (Lynch 2007). Even for genuine adaptations, saying the wing is a "reproductive organ" collapses Tinbergen's distinct questions of function, mechanism, development, and history into one word (Tinbergen 1963). The essay elsewhere insists on keeping these levels apart; the opening joke is a category error it spends the rest of the piece warning against.
